query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of aluminum (≈1 at.%) to a refractory high-entropy alloy will improve its high-temperature oxygen resistance by promoting the in-situ formation of a continuous, adherent alumina scale that slows oxygen ingress.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., equiatomic Ti-V-Nb-Ta or similar composition) without aluminum doping, which typically forms an unprotected oxide scale at high temperatures.
generation.intervention: Alloy modification by incorporating approximately 1 atomic percent of aluminum into the base refractory high-entropy alloy formulation.
generation.conditions: Exposure at temperatures in the range of 700–900°C in an oxidizing atmosphere (air with controlled oxygen partial pressure) for extended durations (e.g., 100 hours).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a uniform, slow-growing, and adherent Al2O3 (alumina) surface layer that acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion.
generation.mechanism: During high-temperature exposure, the added aluminum preferentially migrates to the surface where it oxidizes to form a protective alumina layer. This barrier reduces further oxygen penetration and minimizes internal oxidation and degradation relative to the untreated alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the undoped alloy, the aluminum-doped alloy is expected to show a significant reduction (on the order of at least 30% lower oxidation weight gain) and a thinner, more protective oxide layer under identical high-temperature, oxidizing conditions.
generation.baseline: The oxidation performance (e.g., weight gain and scale thickness) of the original refractory HEA without aluminum under identical thermal and atmospheric exposure.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is anticipated only within a specific aluminum concentration window (around 1 at.%); higher aluminum contents might lead to brittle intermetallics or deleterious phase formation. Moreover, the protective alumina scale is expected to form only at sufficiently high temperatures (≥700°C) in oxidizing environments, so the effect may not be significant at lower temperatures or in inert atmospheres.
generation.uncertainty: While the mechanism is well established in other high-temperature alloys, the optimal aluminum content and its impact on other mechanical properties (e.g., ductility and phase stability) in refractory HEAs remain to be determined experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the base refractory HEA and one set with ~1 at.% aluminum added. Expose both sets to an oxidizing atmosphere at 800°C for 100 hours. After exposure, measure and compare the oxidation weight gains, oxide scale thickness (using cross-sectional electron microscopy), and phase composition (using X-ray diffraction).
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and uniformity via microscopy
Phase analysis of the oxide layer via XRD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminum-doped alloy does not exhibit at least a 30% reduction in oxidation weight gain and demonstrably thinner, more protective oxide scale compared to the undoped baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The presence of intermetallic compounds, such as brittle Laves phases, typically reduces the ductility of RHEAs (), prompting extensive efforts to develop single-phase RHEAs for high-temperature applications (, , , , , , ). The equiatomic Ti-V-Nb-Ta alloy is one of the most attractive RHEAs, which solidifies as a single-phase body-centered cubic (BCC) microstructure with heterogeneous elemental distribution and exhibits excellent high-temperature strength and room-temperature ductility (). Equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta has an extremely high compressive yield strength, 1273 MPa at room temperature and 688 MPa at 900°C (). By comparison, conventional high-temperature Ni-base superalloys notably soften above 600°C, with the compressive yield strength dropping to ~200 MPa at 900°C (). Equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta also exhibits impressive tensile ductility, ~14% at room temperature (), and a relatively low brittle-to-ductile transition temperature between −47° and −27°C, comparable to BCC metals and stainless steels for engineering applications (, ). In this work, the formation of carbide with the concertation of carbon at 0.1 at.% in refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) Mo15Nb20Re15Ta30W20 was studied under both ambient and high-pressure high-temperature conditions. The x-ray diffraction of dilute carbon (C)-doped RHEA under ambient pressure showed that the phases and lattice constant of RHEA were not influenced by the addition of 0.1 at.% C. In contrast, C-doped RHEA showed unexpected phase formation and transformation under combined high-pressure and high-temperature conditions by resistively employing the heated diamond anvil cell (DAC) technique. The new FCC_L12 phase appeared at 6 GPa and 809 °C and preserved the ambient temperature and pressure. High-pressure and high-temperature promoted the formation of carbides Ta3C and Nb3C, which are stable and may further improve the mechanical performance of the dilute C-doped alloy Mo15Nb20Re15Ta30W20.
